title: Meconium Aspiration Syndrome
subject: Paediatrics
summary: A term infant with meconium‐contaminated fluid develops respiratory distress, hypoxaemia and sometimes persistent pulmonary hypertension. Early recognition and supportive care are key.

sections.p: MAS is the inhalation of meconium into the lungs during labour, causing airway obstruction, chemical pneumonitis and hypoxaemia. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by chest radiograph showing patchy infiltrates and a history of meconium staining.
b: Respiratory distress within minutes of birth

t.b: Shows diffuse ground‑glass or patchy infiltrates; confirms pulmonary involvement and rules out congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
Assesses oxygenation; PaO2 < 50 mmHg or PaCO2 > 60 mmHg indicates severe hypoxaemia.
Detects SpO2 < 90% on room air; guides need for oxygen or ventilation.

sections.p: The Greenfield staging classifies MAS into mild, moderate and severe based on clinical and radiographic findings.
b: Moderate: tachypnoea, SpO2 85–90%, chest X‑ray infiltrates
Severe: severe distress, SpO2 < 85%, need for ventilation or PPHN

sections.p: The primary cause is meconium passage into the amniotic fluid, usually after fetal distress. In low‑resource settings, prematurity, maternal infection and delayed cord clamping can worsen outcomes.
b: Fetal distress (e.g., prolonged labour, fetal heart rate decelerations)

t.b: Rule out malaria as a cause of fetal distress; positive result suggests need for antimalarial treatment.
Positive maternal HIV increases risk of prematurity and neonatal infection; informs prophylaxis.

sections.p: Within minutes of birth the infant shows tachypnoea, grunting, cyanosis and sometimes a characteristic greenish sputum. The chest may be hyperinflated or show air trapping.

t.b: SpO2 < 90% on room air signals need for oxygen.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, focus on bedside tests. Full blood count, CRP and cultures are useful if infection is suspected.

t.b: Detects neutropenia or thrombocytopenia, which may indicate sepsis.
Elevated CRP supports bacterial infection; normal CRP suggests non‑infectious MAS.
Positive culture guides antibiotic choice; negative culture does not rule out infection.

sections.p: PPHN, pneumothorax, sepsis and bronchopulmonary dysplasia are serious complications. Watch for worsening hypoxaemia, persistent tachypnoea and abnormal chest sounds.
b: PPHN: sudden drop in SpO2 despite oxygen
Sepsis: fever, lethargy, abnormal blood counts

t.b: Detects wheeze, crackles or absent breath sounds; guides need for imaging.
Rapid decline suggests PPHN or pneumothorax.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide respiratory support and monitor for complications. Avoid drugs that worsen pulmonary hypertension.
b: If severe, intubate and ventilate with low tidal volume
Use inhaled nitric oxide if available for PPHN

t.b: Reduces pulmonary vascular resistance in PPHN; avoid if not available.
Consider if surfactant deficiency is suspected; not routinely used in MAS.
Start empiric broad‑spectrum if sepsis suspected; avoid aminoglycosides if renal function is impaired.

sections.p: Monitor for chronic lung disease and neurodevelopment. Prevention focuses on early detection of fetal distress and prompt delivery.

t.b: Ensure airway patency and suctioning of meconium before ventilation.

sections.p: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia and sepsis can mimic MAS.
b: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: bowel loops in chest on X‑ray

sections.p: A normal chest X‑ray early on may miss MAS; delayed imaging can show infiltrates later. Pulse oximetry may be falsely normal if probe is on a dark skin tone.

t.b: If clinical suspicion remains high despite normal initial X‑ray.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe respiratory distress with SpO2 < 85% despite oxygen
Sudden worsening of breathing or cyanosis

faq.q: Why is suctioning of meconium done before ventilation?
faq.a: It removes thick meconium from the airway, reducing obstruction and preventing aspiration into lower airways.

faq.q: When is inhaled nitric oxide indicated?
faq.a: In persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn that does not improve with oxygen and ventilation.

faq.q: What is the main difference between MAS and sepsis?
faq.a: MAS presents immediately after birth with respiratory distress; sepsis may develop later and is associated with fever and abnormal blood counts.

exam: What is the first step in managing a term infant with suspected MAS? — Suction airway, give oxygen, assess SpO2.
How would you differentiate MAS from congenital diaphragmatic hernia on chest X‑ray? — Look for bowel loops in chest.
Why is surfactant therapy not routinely used in MAS? — MAS is not primarily a surfactant deficiency; surfactant is reserved for RDS.
When is inhaled nitric oxide indicated in MAS? — Persistent hypoxaemia with PPHN despite oxygen and ventilation.
What red flag would prompt immediate intubation? — SpO2 < 85% despite 100% oxygen or sudden drop in SpO2.
Why avoid aminoglycosides in a neonate with MAS? — They can cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; use alternatives if renal function is compromised.
related: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn
